Traverser la pandémie grâce à la communa: Getting through the pandemic with the help of community
Un vendredi matin, les gens font la file: On a Friday morning, people line up on the sidewalk outside Cheskie’s, the famous kosher bakery in the Mile End.
Mayer Feig, porte-parole du Conseil des: Mayer Feig, spokesperson for the Council of Hasidic Jews of Quebec, in front of the Lipa kosher grocery. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
J'habite non loin de la boulangerie Ches: I live not far from Cheskie’s bakery. When I learned that police had handed out tickets to people at religious gatherings in synagogues in the neighbourhood, I contacted Cheskie’s family at the bakery to ask whether they knew anything about what had happened, or whether they had concerns to share on behalf of the wider community.
Je suis profondément reconnaissante à Ch: I am deeply grateful to Cheskie and his family for the way they agreed to speak with me. They invited me into the back of the bakery, and then into their home, to explain their concerns and give me their views. Throughout the preparation of this article, I was struck by the feeling of being truly in the thick of the story, especially as we all continue to live with the uncertainty caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Because my father is Jewish, I am familiar with many Jewish customs and traditions, but I am not Hasidic. I had a hard time approaching the community in the neighbourhood, because many Hasidic Jews are hesitant to speak to outsiders, as well as to the media, given the distorted portrayal of them in the mainstream media. When I began working on this story in January, I committed to meeting as many people as possible and to writing the report in the most open and fair-minded way I could, giving myself enough time to look into the issues the community would bring to me.
Cela a été particulièrement difficile, c: This was particularly difficult, because I had to grapple with the many very complex aspects of the relationships between communities that live together, but differently. Stereotypes, hatred, misunderstanding and poor communication were topics of discussion with my sources, and even though they were often hard to talk about, these discussions were enriching in themselves and helped bridge gaps. It was especially difficult to get municipal authorities to speak about what is being done to defend the community’s interests at the provincial level, since that is where COVID-19 regulations are put in place. However, the many conversations I had with members of the different communities certainly helped me understand that COVID-19 did not mark the beginning of these communication problems and probably will not mark their end. Every person I spoke with stressed the importance of respect and the need for ongoing communication.
Au cours de notre conversation téléphoni: During our phone conversation, Professor Frédéric Dejean and I talked about the pandemic as an “apocalypse” – a word from the Greek that literally means “to uncover” – and about how it has changed or revealed many dimensions of our lives, for better, but also for worse. I dare hope that these revelations will teach us to live together better.
À l'intérieur règne une atmosphère très: Inside, the atmosphere is lively; people weave past one another, pointing out loaves of challah, chocolate chip cookies and triangular hamentashen. Behind the counter, you often find Cheskie himself, his wife Malky or one of their five daughters, serving the uninterrupted stream of customers coming through the door in English, French, Hebrew and Yiddish. Cheskie’s is a Heimishe bakery – a Yiddish word meaning “welcoming” that indicates the establishment sells kosher products intended for the Hasidic community. Yet every day, the bakery is full of people of diverse origins and cultures, ordering slices of babka or an assortment of colourful sugar cookies coated in chocolate and sprinkles.
Des clients à la boulangerie Cheskie. Ph: Customers at Cheskie’s bakery. Photo: Cara Fox
Cheskie Lebowitz est un homme de petite:
Cheskie Lebowitz is a small man with gentle eyes that light up above his mask. It hides only part of his long beard. He is quiet but energetic, moving from one end of the bakery to the other, making sure everything runs perfectly. Since the start of the pandemic, a sign on the front door has read: “Maximum seven people.” “Generally speaking, business is going well,” says Cheskie, slipping into the back kitchen among a team of three or four masked employees who cut, pack and stack mountains of boxes of rugelach and cheesecake.

However, there has been a noticeable increase in antisemitism and police activity in the neighbourhood since the start of COVID-19, he tells us. Cheskie says he was there a few months ago when police showed up at the nearby synagogue, where people had gathered to pray. He tried to talk with the officers to defuse the tense situation, but to no avail. The incident was later attributed to communication problems between the provincial government, regional public health and the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal.
Libby, l'une des filles de Cheskie, est: Libby, one of Cheskie’s daughters, is a journalist. She is currently writing an article on COVID-19 restrictions because she believes there needs to be a broader discussion about government accountability and the communication of emergency and extralegal decrees.
« Les gens pensent qu'on ne veut pas sui: “People think we don’t want to follow the rules, or that we don’t care about people,” she says, commenting on the way the media have portrayed Hasidic communities in Outremont since the start of the pandemic. “But that’s not the point,” she adds. “It’s about continuing to live. It’s our way of life.”
Comme pour toutes les communautés montré: As with all Montréal communities, the health crisis forced Hasidim to change their way of life in order to comply with the new rules. For example, when the province closed places of worship early in the pandemic, the neighbourhood made international headlines because people there organized to pray together in the street.
À mesure que le gouvernement a mis en pl: As the government introduced and changed restrictions, the new decrees began to affect people in unexpected ways. For instance, a higher proportion of large Hasidic families were caught up in problems at first, when distancing measures were introduced. Some were reportedly falsely accused of violating physical distancing laws.
Plus récemment, le couvre-feu provincial: More recently, the provincial curfew has created problems for observing religious traditions and rituals, including the celebration of the Sabbath, which must take place after sunset.
Lorsque Québec a imposé et modifié les r: When Quebec imposed and changed restrictions on gatherings in places of worship, the confusion was even greater, since no one knew whether the number of people allowed to gather depended on the room (as in other decrees) or on the entire building.
« C'est normal de poser des questions, c: “It’s normal to ask questions, it’s normal to be upset and confused,” says Libby, exasperated, as she explains how the pandemic has affected her and her family over the past year.
« Il y a une raison valable, car tout n':
“There’s a valid reason, because not everything is clear,” she adds.

Besides calling for more clarity and transparency in COVID-19 legislation, Libby would like more attention paid to how certain restrictions infringe on rights guaranteed by the Charter, such as freedom of religion.
« Le gouvernement a dit à un certain mom: “At one point the government said theatres were allowed to open with 200 people inside, but synagogues were only allowed to open with 10 people inside,” she says.
“C'est mon droit de pratiquer ma religio: “It’s my right to practise my religion, more than going to the theatre, no?” she asks.
« Il est extrêmement difficile de compre: “It is extremely hard to understand what we’re supposed to do, what they expect of us,” adds Mayer Feig, spokesperson for the Council of Hasidic Jews of Quebec. According to him, the council has been in contact with government representatives through interfaith consultations since June, and yet misunderstandings persist.
« Il y a quelques mois, pendant la deuxi: “A few months ago, during the second wave, when we were still allowed 25 people per room, in accordance with Public Health rules, officers would show up at a synagogue and say, ‘You’re only allowed one person per building.’ Then they’d go to another place and say, ‘You’re allowed 6 people per building,’ or ‘You’re allowed 25 people per building,’ or else ‘You’re allowed 25 people per room.’ So they were going in every direction,” he recalls.
Selon M. Feig, les agents qui se présent: According to Mr. Feig, the officers who showed up at synagogues claimed to be applying Public Health recommendations, but their instructions directly contradicted what the ministry had communicated to officials.
« Nous nous sommes adressés aux gens de: “We went to the Public Health people and said we had agreements with them about what we were supposed to do, but the SPVM says otherwise. We asked them for clarification. Sometimes the measures were clarified but never implemented; sometimes they were never clarified,” he explains.
Le service des relations avec les médias: The SPVM’s media relations office would neither confirm nor deny these allegations and declined to comment on any details of its interventions with, or communications with, the Hasidic community of Outremont.
M. Feig affirme que, aujourd'hui, compte: Mr. Feig says that today, given the drop in the infection rate in the community, he would like the restrictions affecting places of worship to be reassessed. “There is no evidence and there is no case on record of a COVID-19 outbreak or epidemic being traced to a place of worship,” he says.
Selon Santé Montréal, 93 % des foyers ac: According to Santé Montréal, 93% of active outbreaks were instead located in <l1>workplaces, schools, care homes and security services</l1>, many of which remain open.
« Si on peut le faire en toute sécurité,: “If we can do it safely, why not?” Mr. Feig asks about religious gatherings. “It’s a protection provided for in our Charter of Rights.”
« Il est possible de procéder en toute s: “It is possible to do it safely,” he continues. “A great many manufacturing businesses and schools, which are far greater spreaders of the virus, continue to operate, which is understandable, because they are essential. Prayer is essential for us. As essential as alcohol, flowers, cannabis and many other things that are allowed.”
Une feuille à l’entrée d’une synagogue a: A sheet of paper at the entrance to a synagogue jokingly announces that it is a theatre, pointing out that if the building were a theatre, it could hold more than 10 people. Photo: Alain Picard
Frédéric Dejean, professeur en sciences: Frédéric Dejean, a professor of religious studies at the Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM), says the concerns voiced in Outremont reflect a broader issue for all religious traditions in Quebec.
« C'est une question de communication in: “It’s a question of intercultural communication,” he says, explaining that the province’s commitment to secularism makes things difficult and complicated to address.
« Il est difficile de maintenir l'équili: “It’s hard to maintain a balance between religious freedom and the general interest,” he continues. “And people outside these communities often don’t understand why, in certain situations, people place religious law above government edicts.”
M. Dejean, qui a récemment coécrit un ar: Mr. Dejean, who recently co-wrote an article advocating greater sensitivity in enforcing limits on religious gatherings in communities like Outremont’s, believes it is essential that people outside the communities make an effort to better understand differences in perspective and daily life if they wish to improve the situation.
« Cette crise est un indicateur de la fa: “This crisis is an indicator of how we view religious groups and religious issues in Quebec these days,” he says. “Lessons have been learned from this situation, and I hope those lessons won’t be forgotten in the future.”
Fanny Magini, conseillère d'arrondisseme: Fanny Magini, a borough councillor in Outremont, says her office is aware of the problems that exist in the borough. She agrees that better communication is needed. “I think there was a lot of confusion, and unfortunately, what happened happened,” she says of the police interventions and conflicts that took place in January.
Mme Magini affirme que son cabinet ne re: Ms. Magini says her office receives no direct communication from the province about new decrees. She has no way of knowing whether, or when, the government will impose further restrictions.
Elle ajoute néanmoins que, depuis son él: She adds, however, that since her election in 2017, her team has tried to build ties with Outremont’s Hasidic communities, including by distributing City communications in English and French and promoting City events and news in community publications like the <l1>Heimishe News Flash</l1> in order to encourage more citizens to take part in local political life.
En ce qui concerne le fait que les restr: As for the fact that COVID-19 restrictions disproportionately affect certain religious communities in the borough, Ms. Magini says the problem is a matter of priorities. “There is a majority view about what is essential. For example, the SAQ and the SQDC are considered essential. But for these communities, what’s essential is to pray,” she says.
« Est-ce que ce que la majorité pense êt: “Is what the majority thinks is essential really essential? And does the majority take the needs of the minority into account?” she asks. “It’s a philosophical question.”
Une question philosophique aux conséquen: A philosophical question with very real consequences for those living that reality – and one to which Ms. Magini, unfortunately, offers no solution.
En revanche, en tant que présidente du C: On the other hand, as chair of the City of Montréal’s Culture and Commerce Committee, she says she is working on implementing a major new cultural plan for the borough. The plan has been the subject of public consultations and hearings for a year, and she urges all members of the community to take part.
« Il est certain que [les contributions: “It is certain that [the contributions of the Hasidic communities] is an element we want to see in the cultural plan that will be implemented over the next five years,” she says. She adds that interested people can contact the City by <l1>visiting the borough’s website</l1> or its <l2>Facebook page</l2>, or by subscribing to the borough’s <l3>newsletter</l3>.
Pendant ce temps, la boulangerie est plo: Meanwhile, the bakery is plunged into darkness as Cheskie and his family celebrate Passover, a holiday that requires the entire shop and kitchen to be cleaned from top to bottom, and any remaining chametz, or leaven residue, to be eliminated.
La boulangerie restera fermée jusqu'au 2: The bakery will remain closed until April 2, while the local Jewish community celebrates the holiday with Seder meals, songs, traditional foods and games.
Avec les restrictions sanitaires imposée: With the health restrictions imposed by the government, Libby says many people will be weighing the risks of spending time with their families during this important holiday.
S'il va de soi que la loi doit être resp: While it goes without saying that the law must be respected, life goes on.
« Ce n'est pas une vie de peur, dit Libb: “It’s not a life of fear,” says Libby. “It’s a life of family and community.”
